rationale: The fig-and-almond syrup arm recorded three tremor events among 40 children versus zero among 40 in each comparator arm. All participants took methylphenidate and the groups differed in formulation. The adverse reports lack a rest-tremor definition and the population differs from Parkinson disease. Gafoor's recovered article tests a concentrated dried-fruit extract against motor tasks in rats, with numeric table cells still missing. The fig-containing walnut-bar experiment tests a baked mixture and measures catalepsy and coordination, without isolating fig or measuring rest tremor. The Parkinson diet shares figs across groups. The checked Unani composition names peepal, a different species. A separable raw common-fig effect on Parkinson rest tremor remains open. Four full originals concern clinical or sensor work without raw fig intake. The Chitrakoot field inventory documents fig fruit use for constipation without individual response, leaving the rest tremor question open. Five additional originals concern multiple system atrophy, genetic parkinsonism, rehabilitation, spinal stimulation or an experimental compound. None measures raw fig exposure, leaving the rest tremor effect open. The Parkinson probiotic review and environmental exposure article contain no measured raw fig intake or associated rest tremor outcome. The three newly checked originals address walking tremor, clinical tremor phenotypes or experimental neural recordings. They do not relate raw fig exposure to rest tremor. A fig-fruit extract toxicity study lists tremor in a general surveillance checklist and gives no separate event or rest-tremor estimate. Fresh fig allergy case histories concern a different outcome.

The 21-person whole dried Ajwa crossover reported near-identical abdominal pain diary means, and the pediatric whole-date and mouse comparisons did not clearly separate groups. Date syrups had favorable labor-pain observations with preparation, comparator and population limits. The 34-person date-seed exercise trial reported lower pain at 24 hours (3.35 vs 5.00 on a 0–10 scale, p<.001), with an inconclusive immediate contrast. Its companion biomarkers belong to the same cohort. Parkinson bar studies supply whole-product or composite outcomes without an attributable date-paste and pain comparison. Separate public accounts recall less abdominal pain or more discomfort after date fruit, without an established Parkinson diagnosis or controlled exposure. Extract results are confounded by sedation. No observed study direction transfers defensibly to whole dried-date intake and pain severity in Parkinson disease. The fresh Rutab trial pooled 76 labor-pain categories across arms, and the late-pregnancy whole-fruit comparison reports labor progression without a pain score. Two favorable syrup trials are independent of each other, while the two Khorramabad reports share participants. The later review could not pool a pain estimate. Spanish ethnobotanical and historical sources document intended fruit analgesia and postpartum use without observed patient change or known drying state. None of these sources supplies enough transfer for a dried-date effect on Parkinson pain. In a quasi-experimental study, laboring women allowed dates, orange juice and water had less late-stage pain than a fasting group. Food choice and the ingredient effect were unresolved. Another small report from the same hospital gives labor progress and unstratified analgesic use. The two reports may overlap. The 64-person Persian date-syrup report has the same registration as the 80-person report. Its 30-minute comparison was inconclusive and the 60-minute VAS favored syrup. Five of six control VAS rows match exactly between the companion honey and date reports, leaving participant mapping open. None of these data isolate a whole dried-date effect in Parkinson pain. Newly checked whole-date case narratives describe possible abdominal pain in a family with hereditary fructose intolerance. Two relatives received fructose testing, independently of food exposure. Oral pollen data show less treatment-related mouth pain in sequentially allocated oncology groups. A seed powder case gives a distinct adverse event estimate of 8/10 abdominal pain at presentation. The small Zahidi flesh crossover reports only biomarkers, and the colitis study tests pollen extract in animals. These observations preserve both signs at their actual preparation, endpoint and population. The near-null Ajwa diary comparison and indirect labor, seed and cultural reports leave the dried-fruit Parkinson pain effect open. The complete 2026 pollen original assigns the Figure 2 finding to fecal occult blood. Pain was not a measured outcome. Forty-five new checked publications do not provide dried date fruit exposure for Parkinson pain. The 2015 Unani review documents pain-related indications and a headache caution, with no identified fruit drying state or reported comparable clinical response. The date fruit effect remains open. Thirty-nine newly checked originals do not include dried date fruit as an exposure for clinical Parkinson pain. The earlier human, experimental and cultural source distinctions remain material. Original arthritis and edema reports have distinct edible-fruit extract and seed preparations, with no stand-alone pain severity contrast. The migraine distillate registration still supplies no results. A premenstrual date-fruit trial abstract reports improvement of cramps without a comparative pain-severity estimate, verified drying status or a Parkinson cohort. The reviewing article is a secondary citation trail.

A randomized active-oil comparison in 140 adults with functional constipation favored raw extra-virgin over refined olive oil on constipation and stool form. It excluded neurological causes. The Albacete original shows a favorable association for virgin olive oil, contrary to a secondary review classification, with only 11 low consumers and no controlled Parkinson analysis. MEDI-PD and the independent Fernandez waitlist trial found inconclusive Parkinson whole-diet comparisons. Fernandez measured olive oil within dietary adherence and did not assign isolated oil or grade. The ulcerative-colitis crossover between-oil result and an isolated Parkinson trial remain open. The matched active-oil comparison supports a minimal easing lean. A synucleinopathy review explicitly lists extra-virgin olive oil as customary constipation advice without a trial at the time of publication. Its separate fermented milk comparison does not estimate olive oil. This provides no additional directional estimate. The two microbiome reviews describe the olive-oil food-frequency association and Mediterranean dietary context. They do not add an independent extra-virgin olive-oil constipation comparison to the existing clinical record. Publisher Figure 2 now confirms lower constipation severity after extra-virgin olive oil than after canola oil in the 32-person ulcerative colitis crossover (paired p<.001). This supplements the independent functional-constipation comparison and is eligible as a limited indirect easing signal because the exposure and symptom fit. Its magnitude, tolerability, period and order effects remain unresolved. The planned COLONIC trial is a separate registry record without outcomes. No isolated Parkinson estimate is available, so keep the minimal signal. The review separately discusses constipation in Parkinson disease and olive oil within a Mediterranean pattern. It supplies no comparison of extra-virgin olive oil for constipation. The earlier active-oil trial outside Parkinson disease remains the closest directional evidence. The 2022 gut-brain review places olive oil in a wider dietary pattern and supplies no grade-specific constipation estimate. The flavonoids review mentions olive oil within a dietary pattern. It adds no isolated extra-virgin olive oil constipation result beyond the earlier comparisons. The Parkinson phase Ib study recorded one constipation event in a three-person active formulation arm. Olive oil carried compounds in every arm, and grade and constipation severity were not compared. The autonomic review identifies its extra-virgin olive-oil dietary suggestion as untested. The earlier oil comparison remains the closest evidence. The Bahrami surgical trial author abstract gives a favorable bowel comparison for extra-virgin olive oil versus usual care, with no full estimates or stool-score definition. The NHANES association comes from a dietary composite and total fat ratio. The Fernandez randomized Parkinson whole-diet result was inconclusive between arms and its final abstract shares the preprint cohort. These sources do not elevate the minimal easing anchor from the functional-constipation comparison. Fieldwork from the Aydin region describes fig and olive oil used together for stomach discomfort, and the paper cites a combined use for constipation. The oil grade and symptom change are unavailable.

Three independent randomized human trials outside Parkinson disease report lower visual-analogue pain with encapsulated oral cinnamon bark powder versus starch placebo in primary dysmenorrhea (n=114, 24-72 h), migraine (n=43 completers, p<.001), and rheumatoid arthritis (n=36, abstract p<.001), alongside a high-attrition multiple-sclerosis trial with baseline imbalance and endpoint switch (VAS vs registered PQAS). Competing controlled trials show null upper abdominal pain for cinnamon-sesame macerate versus sesame oil and inconsistent exercise-soreness findings, while the single Parkinson rehabilitation case combined cassia with multimodal therapy. One oral ground Ceylon cinnamon experiment in female rats found smaller bladder-distension reflexes with induced cystitis and larger responses in uninflamed bladders at the same higher dose. The mixed animal proxy supplies no transferable sign. Differences in culinary ground exposure, non-Parkinson pain etiologies, and reporting limits keep the favorable easing signal at minimal_signal. An identified Cinnamomum burmannii extract in a cellular screen supplies preparation context without a pain-severity or Parkinson observation. Cinnamon is an identification odor in the acute-illness comparison. The paper has no assigned culinary cinnamon pain treatment or attributable pain contrast. The review lists cinnamon as one source of eugenol. Isolated-eugenol trials have chemical, thermal and motor results in rodents, with controlled human oral cinnamon evidence still the closest basis. The new experiment concerns an isolated cinnamon constituent in an animal model with intestinal outcomes. Ground cinnamon and clinical Parkinson pain were not assessed. A traceable Chinese consensus passage recommends a compound cinnamon-twig formula with kudzu as one patterned pain option. Its recommendation supplies no measured result for ground cinnamon in people with Parkinson disease. An extract adjunct trial in H. pylori treatment reports lower short-term epigastric-pain prevalence (p=.02 in Table 2), while a different combined cinnamon leaf tea pilot reports transient colicky pain without a quantified comparison. The contexts and exposures limit transfer to ground bark and Parkinson pain. A separate trial of cinnamon powder mixed in water reports lower menstrual pain than empty capsules in three cycles. The erratum reconciles 107 randomized and 99 analyzed. Unblinded comparison, baseline-table anomalies and a different pain condition keep the existing minimal tier.
